name: Pnar
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand sources agree (3 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final (final stress)' rests on Ring 2015, the xxii+694-pp NTU reference grammar that heads Glottolog's list for pnar1238. We held no copy; I downloaded the thesis (Internet Archive copy of the NTU bitstream named in the record) and confirmed the deciding quotation verbatim at sec. 2.3.5, printed p. 56. The same work restates final-syllable primary stress as the defining property of the phonological word (pp. 60-61), notes longer vowels in stressed final syllables (p. 54), and self-codes WALS 14A = Ultimate, 15A = no weight sensitivity, 17A = no rhythmic stress (p. 572). Two further open sources by the same describer were downloaded and agree: Ring 2012 MKS 40 (pp. 142, 153: final syllables take primary stress) and Ring & Anderson 2018 JSEALS SP3 (p. 16: iambic, strong stress on the word-final syllable, F0 the primary correlate; pilot acoustic data pp. 22-25, 30 show pitc

sources.citation: Ring 2015, A grammar of Pnar, PhD thesis NTU (Internet Archive copy of dr.ntu.edu.sg bitstream), sec. 2.3.5, full text read
sources.quote: Stress is the main means of distinguishing word boundaries in Pnar. The final syllable of a word carries heavier stress than preceding syllables, creating minor-major syllable pairings. This provides strong evidence for deciding whether or not clitics and other grammatical morphemes are constituents of a word

sources.quote: 'Stress is the main means of distinguishing word boundaries in Pnar. The final syllable of a word carries heavier stress than preceding syllables, creating minor-major syllable pairings.' (p. 56); 'a phonological word always retains primary stress on its final syllable, indicating a word boundary' (p. 60); appendix p. 572: 14A Fixed Stress = Ultimate; 15A no weight-sensitivity; 17A no rhythmic stress.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 16: 'In Pnar (Ring 2015a, b), as in Khasian languages generally (Rabel 1961; Nagaraja 1985), word stress has been reported as iambic, where strong stress falls on the final syllable of a word. The primary correlate of word stress in Pnar is pitch (F0)... Other correlates of stress include duration ... and intensity.' Pilot acoustic study (1097 words from a Pnar narrative): 2- and 3-syllable words show pitch rise to the final syllable (pp. 22-23, 30); 4-syllable words show two peaks, interpreted as two phonological words 'each with final-syllable stress' (p. 25).
sources.locator: p. 16 (PDF p. 24); sec. 3.2 pp. 22-25; conclusion p. 30
